evidence.note: 39's table distinguishes disabled from enabled modes but omits pending-request semantics. pthread_cancel documents queuing until re-enabling, with the cancellation type then determining delivery.

correction.note: The disabled request stays pending rather than merely possibly pending. Timing after re-enable depends on cancellation type.

evidence.note: 41 directly labels CLONE_VM as sharing the same memory space.

correction.note: Use the other clone sharing flags as distractors.

evidence.note: 41 independently identifies sharing of open files with CLONE_FILES and memory with CLONE_VM. Under the stated combination only the former sharing is requested.

correction.note: Distinguish parent and child of one successful clone, and sharing the table from mere inherited entries.

evidence.note: 10's equation gives (100−75)×2=50 ms of one-core parallel work, hence 50 ms of serial work and S=0.50.

correction.note: State the one-core baseline explicitly before using the inverse Amdahl calculation.

evidence.note: 31 bounds threads separately from outstanding work. Given the stem's unbounded queue, these queued jobs can still consume additional memory.
2 motivates synchronizing shared data; 9 calls an outcome that changes with execution order a race condition.

correction.note: Use mechanisms that could account for scheduling behavior instead of unrelated concepts.

evidence.note: 7–9 show read/modify/write as separate operations. Applying the shown interleaving to two increments from 10 produces two writes of 11.
7 gives the increment/decrement operations, and 9 explicitly notes the result 6 when the producer's write is last.
7 and 9 supply the read/modify/write steps. With the complete first operation preceding the second read, 5 becomes 6 and then 5.

correction.note: State explicitly that the second operation is one decrement, and classify the short serial trace as intermediate.

evidence.note: 7 decomposes count++ into separate steps. 18 contrasts this with purpose-built atomic read/modify/write instructions.

correction.note: Replace unrelated distractors with actual atomicity misconceptions.

evidence.note: 10 gives shared variable and table updates as critical-section examples; 11 includes shared structures in the protected body.
11 depicts entry, critical section, exit and remainder in that order. The revised stem starts the loop at the entry protocol.

correction.note: The loop can be rotated logically. Anchor the ordering at the entry protocol.

evidence.note: 12 says no second process may be in the corresponding critical section while the first is there.

correction.note: Use concurrency properties as credible alternatives and isolate simultaneous entry.

evidence.note: 12 defines progress as selecting a waiting entrant without indefinite postponement while the shared section is empty.

correction.note: Specify that the forbidden delay concerns selection while nobody is inside, removing distracting overlap with bounded service.

evidence.note: 12 bounds the number of intervening admissions after a request. 20 contrasts this with an unfair basic lock.

correction.note: Bounded waiting is stated in admissions by others, not as an elapsed time limit.

evidence.note: 12 requires progress and 14 uses turn as an arbiter alongside expressed interest. A strict-turn model without the flag cannot advance in the given case.

correction.note: State that only the holder can pass the turn on exit, and distinguish progress from exclusion.

evidence.note: 13 distinguishes preemptible and nonpreemptible kernel execution. Its Turkish shorthand is awkward, so the item states the shared scheduling property.

correction.note: Phrase as the preemption capability, with neighboring scheduling policies as distractors.

evidence.note: 13 gives the kernel-preemption contrast but does not qualify its single-active-process claim. 17 explicitly warns the local scheme is insufficient on multiprocessors.

correction.note: Scope nonpreemption to per-CPU scheduling, qualifying the deck's uniprocessor shorthand.

evidence.note: 14 sets flag[i] before the wait, and 15 keeps it true until the exit assignment. It indicates a request or current use.

correction.note: Contrast the flag's request/lifetime with ownership and priority.

evidence.note: 14/15 show while(flag[j] && turn == j). Both conjuncts are true in the stated snapshot, so Pi waits.

correction.note: State the abstract algorithm's memory model and use precise possible transitions.

evidence.note: 14/15 show a conjunction, so false flag[j] defeats waiting even with turn still equal to j. This qualifies the prose shortcut on 15.

correction.note: Treat it as one Boolean guard application and remove impossible unrelated actions.

evidence.note: 14/15 show each process giving the turn to its peer. The final turn=0 permits P0 and keeps P1 waiting when both flags are true.
15's exit resets flag[i], which can end the other process's waiting condition; the peer need not wait for turn to change.

correction.note: Focus the exit behavior on the waiting test and use the actual flag/turn distinction.

evidence.note: 16 says the classic software solution is not guaranteed on modern machines. Linux memory-barrier documentation describes ordering and visibility constraints for shared accesses.

correction.note: Compare the memory-model issue to plausible but insufficient changes in platform design.

evidence.note: 17 restricts interrupt masking to a single-CPU setting for simple protection and explains why it does not apply to multiple CPUs.

correction.note: Make alternatives about the scope of local interrupt masking.

evidence.note: 18's test_and_set saves the previous Boolean, writes true, and returns the saved value. From false, the pair is (false, true).

correction.note: Replace two implausible non-Boolean options with the two Boolean dimensions and distinguish return from stored state.

evidence.note: 18 defines the same transition; two serialized calls without release observe false then true.
19's CAS compares the current value, writes the new value on a match, and returns the old value. Equal 7 changes memory to 9.
19's old-value CAS returns 5 without changing memory because expected 4 differs from 5.
19 waits while the old value returned by CAS(lock,0,1) is nonzero. Returning zero means the free-to-held transition succeeded.

correction.note: Recognizing a single old-value test is intermediate. Clarify that this is the lecture's particular CAS interface.

evidence.note: 16 introduces locking, 18 couples test/set atomically, and 21 illustrates acquire/release. Separating test and write admits two false observations.

correction.note: Specify the precise non-atomic pair, including the first state. Remove the distractor that changes the premises to an atomic admission.

evidence.note: 18 shows mutual exclusion using a basic atomic primitive. 20 says that the basic versions fail bounded waiting and presents an additional protocol.
21 explicitly places acquire before and release after the shared update.

correction.note: Classify recall of the acquire/update/release protocol as basic.

evidence.note: 21 labels the continuously checking acquire loop as busy waiting/spinlock.
21 illustrates checking without blocking and 26 illustrates blocking and later waking. Comparing the remaining wait to the block/wake cost gives the conditional answer.

correction.note: Make the cost comparison conditional and contrast with real spin/block trade-offs.

evidence.note: 23 explicitly initializes a counting semaphore from the number of interchangeable resources. 24 gives the atomically consumed permit.
23/24 describe one decrement per successful wait and one increment per signal. The sequence is 2,1,0,1,0.
23 describes the two-value semaphore. 24 consumes the sole initial permit at the first successful acquisition.

correction.note: Use 'kaynak kullanılmıyorken' instead of the ambiguous empty semaphore wording.

evidence.note: 24 labels signal as V and increments the semaphore while wait (P) obtains a permit.

correction.note: Make distractors operations in the same critical section attempt, not unrelated interrupt operations.

evidence.note: 25 gives a semaphore initialized to zero with S1 preceding signal and wait preceding S2.
25 uses zero to force waiting if B reaches its wait first. An initial one lets B consume a permit before S1 has run.

correction.note: Use plausible permit-order misconceptions in the distractors.

evidence.note: 26 assigns a wait list to the nonspinning design; the conditional-block model clarified in the stem is the intent of 27's acquire sketch.

correction.note: Scope the behavior to a blocking semaphore rather than all semaphore implementations.

evidence.note: 27 gives decrement then queue on value < 0. In the specified model the calls take the count 1→0→−1→−2 and leave two waiters.

correction.note: State the corrected conditional-block model explicitly because the slide's braces make the block placement ambiguous.

evidence.note: 27 gives increment then wake one when the resulting value is ≤0; from −2 that is −1 and one wake.
24 explicitly requires atomic semaphore operations. 27 shows the count change and waiter handling as parts of one semaphore operation.

correction.note: Contrast atomic permit consumption with related but insufficient protections.

evidence.note: 28 depicts opposite order acquisitions of S and Q leading each process to wait for the other.

correction.note: Use neighboring liveness concepts rather than obvious non sequiturs.

evidence.note: 28's counterexample requires opposing order. The revised common order removes the edge where Q is held while S is awaited.

correction.note: Use plausible lock-order protocols rather than nonsensical permanent retention.

evidence.note: 28's cycle depends on a process holding S while requesting Q. Given a nonblocking failed attempt for Q, releasing S before retrying breaks that premise at this step.

correction.note: State that the failed attempt for Q was nonblocking and limit the claim to breaking hold-and-wait at that step.

evidence.note: 30 names indefinite blocking of an older waiter under continuing LIFO service as starvation.

correction.note: Distinguish starvation, deadlock and bounded waiting with realistic classifications.

evidence.note: 28 shows a group with no progress because of a cycle; 30 gives a bypassed waiter in a continuing service system. The stem explicitly excludes a cycle for A.

correction.note: Other unrelated work progressing does not rule out a deadlocked subset. Explicitly state the absence of a cycle and persistent bypass.

evidence.note: 27 shows removing a waiting process, and 30 explains why LIFO can repeatedly bypass an old waiter. Strict FIFO service prevents later arrivals overtaking it.
31 explicitly demonstrates signal-before-entry as a misuse that allows concurrent critical-section entry.

correction.note: Name the counting semaphore used to enforce one entrant and distinguish excess permits from a second blocking wait.

evidence.note: 31 illustrates replacing the post-section signal with a second wait. With no other signal, no permit can become available.

correction.note: Under no other signal, the second wait blocks rather than merely possibly blocking.

evidence.note: 24 assigns permit return to signal. 31 identifies an omitted exit signal as causing blocking if no other permit becomes available.

correction.note: Replace hardware-distraction options with ownership and automatic release misconceptions.

evidence.note: 32 groups shared state and procedures within the monitor's mutual-exclusion construct.

correction.note: Contrast monitor encapsulation with plausible synchronization primitives.

evidence.note: 32 makes exclusion apply to the monitor as a whole. 33 expressly avoids two active monitor participants simultaneously.

correction.note: Make the effect of monitor-wide exclusion explicit and use plausible per-method alternatives.

evidence.note: 33 diagrams blocked and active competitors in the monitor. POSIX condition wait gives a concrete implementation where waiting releases the associated mutex and the return reacquires it.

correction.note: Use mutex or monitor access alternatives rather than unrelated OS resources.

evidence.note: 25 shows semaphore notification creating a permit and 33 describes signalling a waiting condition participant. POSIX explicitly documents no effect with no existing waiter.

correction.note: Distinguish a condition notification from a semaphore permit and use plausible completion conditions.

evidence.note: 33 declares condition variables x and y, with x.signal operating on waiters for x.
33 describes the signal-and-wait signaler waiting for the awakened participant to leave or suspend.

correction.note: Use alternative monitor scheduling disciplines for comparison.

evidence.note: 33 describes signal-and-continue: the signaler retains access until leaving or waiting, and the awakened participant cannot run in the monitor before that.

correction.note: Separate signal-and-continue from immediate handoff and ensure the timing model is specific.

evidence.note: 34 introduces grouped shared updates and 35 defines an atomic block as a transaction. The transactional-memory paper confirms commit/abort all-or-nothing visibility.

correction.note: Use comparable visibility models and keep the claim to transactional writes.

evidence.note: 34–35 motivate transactional memory and show an atomic block but omit conflict handling. Herlihy and Moss sections 2.1–2.2 specify conflict abort and retry of failed operations.

correction.note: Mark conflict handling as supplementary and use alternatives about commit and retry behavior.

evidence.note: 36 shows the critical directive around the shared counter update.

correction.note: Use neighboring OpenMP directives and state the named lecture mechanism.

evidence.note: 36 applies exclusion to the structured statement inside the critical block. The independent local work in the stem is outside that section.

5 shows multiple producers sharing a buffer, 6 describes producer/consumer buffer access, and 21 puts locking around the entire critical update. Two writers can select one slot before the separately protected counter changes.

correction.note: One producer and one consumer can have separate slot pointers. Give two producers competing for a shared free-slot index, making the claimed race concrete.

evidence.note: 23 sets permits equal to resources. 24 increments on each signal, so two signals for one return can create a surplus permit.

correction.note: Use permit-accounting distractors and distinguish over-release from an idempotent unlock.

evidence.note: 10 motivates protecting a common resource and 21's mutex example uses one shared lock for the competing entries.

correction.note: Contrast lock identity with process sharing. State the locks are independent.

evidence.note: 21 demonstrates continuous spinning; 26–27 demonstrate suspension and wakeup. Blocking leaves the CPU available while long waits run.
12 defines exclusion and bounded waiting separately. 20's simple locks show one may be present without the other.

correction.note: Use an explicit bound on intervening admissions, and distinguish all neighboring critical-section criteria.

evidence.note: 10/11 require synchronization on shared objects, and 21 illustrates locking around the complete update. Under the interleaving model an unlocked read can occur between writes.

correction.note: State the abstract interleaving model rather than implying unsynchronized C data races have specified results.

evidence.note: 32–33 demonstrate monitor exclusion and signal-and-continue handoff. The authors' Mesa manual explains why the predicate must be checked again because it may change before resumption.

correction.note: Clarify recheck under the re-acquired lock and the next action when the predicate is false.
